title: Tissues
tagline: Plant tissues — meristematic and permanent — and animal tissues — epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous — their structure and location.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A tissue is a group of cells that are similar in structure and work together to perform a particular function. In multicellular organisms, cells do not all look and act alike — they become specialised into tissues, and tissues are arranged into organs. This chapter studies tissues in plants and in animals separately because their needs are different: a plant is fixed in one place and grows from specific regions, while an animal moves and must be both supported and flexible. In plants the most important division is between meristematic tissue, which can divide, and permanent tissue, which has lost that ability; in animals the main groups are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissue, each with its own task.

facts.value: A tissue is a group of similar cells performing a specific function

facts.label: Animal division

blocks.text: A tissue is a group of cells that are similar in structure and together perform a specific function. For example, the cells lining the inside of the mouth are a tissue that protects and helps in absorption, while the cells in a leaf that make food are another tissue. When several tissues work together to do a more complex job, they form an organ, and organs working together make up an organ system. This organisation — cell, tissue, organ, organ system — is one of the main ideas of biology, because it explains how a very large number of cells can be arranged into an efficient living body.

items.meaning: A group of similar cells that together perform a particular function.
A structure made of several tissues working together to carry out a specific function.
A group of organs working together to perform a major body function.
When cells develop in a particular way to carry out a specific function.

items: A tissue is made of similar cells and performs a specific function.
Tissues are the next level of organisation above the cell.
An organ is made of different tissues working together.
Specialised cells are more efficient at their particular job than unspecialised cells.
Both plants and animals have tissues, but the types differ because their lifestyles differ.

items.text: The lining of the mouth is a protective epithelial tissue.
items.note: It is one simple example of an animal tissue with a clear function.

items.text: A leaf is an organ because it contains epidermal tissue, photosynthetic tissue, vein tissue and others.
items.note: The organ idea is easier to see when one structure clearly contains more than one tissue.

blocks.text: Plants have two broad classes of tissue: meristematic and permanent. Meristematic tissue is made of cells that are actively dividing. These cells are generally small, thin-walled and densely packed with nucleus, and they are found in special growing regions of the plant such as the tips of roots and shoots and in the cambium of stems and roots. Because they divide continuously, meristems are responsible for plant growth. Permanent tissues are those that have been formed from meristematic cells but have lost the ability to divide and have taken on a definite shape, size and function. Permanent tissues may be simple, made of one type of cell, or complex, made of more than one type of cell working together.

items.meaning: Plant tissue made of actively dividing cells, found at growing regions such as root and shoot tips and the cambium.
A region of meristematic tissue; apical meristems are at root and shoot tips, lateral meristems increase girth.
Plant tissue derived from meristematic cells that has lost the power of division and has a definite form and function.
Permanent tissue made of only one type of cell, such as parenchyma, collenchyma or sclerenchyma.
Permanent tissue made of more than one type of cell, such as xylem and phloem.

items: Meristematic cells are small, have dense cytoplasm, a large nucleus and thin walls.
They divide to add new cells, which then become part of the permanent tissues.
Apical meristems are at the tips of roots and shoots and help the plant grow in length.
Lateral meristems, such as the cambium, increase the girth of stems and roots.
Simple permanent tissues include parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
Complex permanent tissues include xylem and phloem, which transport water and food.

learn.title: Animal tissues: the four main types

blocks.text: Animal tissues are usually grouped into four main kinds: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissue. Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces, lines body cavities and forms glands; it is always supported by connective tissue beneath it. Connective tissue connects, supports and binds other tissues and organs, and includes bone, cartilage, blood and adipose tissue. Muscular tissue is responsible for movement and is made of long cells called fibres that can contract. Nervous tissue carries messages through the body and is made of neurons and supporting cells; it is found in the brain, spinal cord and nerves. Together these four tissue types make up the body plan of an animal.

items.meaning: Tissue that covers body surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands; always rests on connective tissue.
A thin layer that anchors epithelial tissue to the connective tissue beneath it.
Tissue that links, supports and protects other tissues and organs; often has cells scattered in a matrix.
Tissue specialised for contraction and movement; made of muscle fibres.
Tissue that transmits impulses; made of neurons and supporting neuroglial cells.
Nerve cell specialised to carry electrical impulses; has a cell body, dendrites and an axon.

items: Epithelial tissue covers and protects, lines cavities, and forms glands.
Epithelium always rests on connective tissue, separated by a basement membrane.
Connective tissue includes bone, cartilage, blood and adipose (fat) tissue.
Bone is a rigid connective tissue with a hard matrix; cartilage is flexible and has a firmer but softer matrix.
Blood is a fluid connective tissue that transports materials around the body.
Muscular tissue brings about movement by contraction.
Nervous tissue transmits messages and coordinates body activities.

items.text: The skin's outer layer is epithelial tissue, protecting the body from the outside.
items.note: Epithelium is the tissue of covering and lining.

items.text: Blood is a connective tissue even though it is liquid, because its cells are carried in a fluid matrix.
items.note: Connective tissue is defined by function and structure, not only by hardness.

items.text: A voluntary muscle like the biceps is made of muscular tissue that contracts to move the arm.
items.note: Muscular tissue is the tissue of active movement.

learn.title: Why plant and animal tissues differ

blocks.text: Plant and animal tissues are organised differently because the organisms face different problems. A plant cannot move from place to place, so many of its tissues are built for support, water transport and food transport, and much of its growth happens only in certain zones where meristematic tissue is present. A plant also has dead supportive tissues such as sclerenchyma, which give strength without needing a blood supply. An animal, by contrast, moves, so it needs muscular tissue for movement, nervous tissue for coordination, and connective tissues such as bone and blood for support, transport and defence. Recognising these differences helps in understanding why a leaf can be stiff without muscles and why an animal body is built around movement and communication.

items: Plants have meristematic tissue for growth at distinct growing points; animals grow more generally.
Many plant support tissues, such as sclerenchyma, are dead at maturity.
Animals have muscular and nervous tissues, which are absent in plants.
Blood is a connective tissue in animals; plants do not have a circulating fluid tissue of the same kind.
Xylem and phloem are the complex transport tissues of plants; blood and lymph perform transport in animals.

items.text: A herbaceous stem stays upright largely because of turgid parenchyma and collenchyma, not because of hard bone.
items.note: Support in plants uses a different tissue strategy from support in animals.

items.text: A nerve carrying a sensation to the brain is nervous tissue, not a plant tissue.
items.note: Nervous tissue is one of the clearest differences between the two kingdoms at tissue level.

assessment.title: Tissues: check your understanding
instructions: Answer the short questions in one or two sentences each.
For the long and analytical questions, write in full sentences and name the tissue types clearly.
All questions are original practice; they are not past paper questions.

exercises.answer: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function.
exercises.explanation: The definition links similar cells and a shared function, which is the essence of a tissue.

exercises.prompt: Give two differences between meristematic tissue and permanent tissue.
exercises.answer: Meristematic tissue is made of actively dividing cells with dense cytoplasm and a large nucleus, while permanent tissue consists of cells that have lost the power to divide and have a definite shape and function. Meristematic cells are generally small and thin-walled, while permanent cells vary widely in structure.
exercises.explanation: Any two clear differences carry the marks; the dividing ability and the structural change are the best ones.

exercises.prompt: Name the three simple permanent tissues of plants and state one function of each.
exercises.answer: Parenchyma stores food and water and, in leaves, helps in photosynthesis; collenchyma provides flexible support in young stems and petioles; sclerenchyma provides rigid support and strength.
exercises.explanation: Each tissue should be named with a distinct function for full marks.

exercises.prompt: Why is blood considered a connective tissue?
exercises.answer: Blood is a connective tissue because it consists of cells (red cells, white cells and platelets) carried in a fluid matrix, and it connects different parts of the body by transporting materials, just as other connective tissues connect, support or bind structures.
exercises.explanation: Blood fits the connective-tissue plan because its cells are suspended in a matrix and it performs linking or transport functions.

exercises.prompt: Name the four main types of animal tissue and give one location of each.
exercises.answer: Epithelial tissue, found in skin and lining organs; connective tissue, found as bone, cartilage, blood and fat; muscular tissue, found in muscles such as the biceps; nervous tissue, found in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.
exercises.explanation: Each tissue should be named with a representative location for full marks.

exercises.prompt: Distinguish parenchyma and sclerenchyma on the basis of cell wall and whether the cells are living or dead.
exercises.answer: Parenchyma has thin cell walls and is made of living cells; sclerenchyma has thick lignified cell walls and its cells are usually dead at maturity.
exercises.explanation: The difference in wall thickness and cell vitality is the key structural contrast.

questions.prompt: A group of similar cells performing a specific function is called a:
questions.explanation: A tissue is a group of similar cells that together perform a particular function; organs are made of tissues.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing organ — an organ is a higher level of organisation made of several tissues.

questions.prompt: Which plant tissue is made of actively dividing cells?
questions.explanation: Meristematic tissue is the dividing tissue of plants, found in growing regions such as root and shoot tips.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing parenchyma — that is a permanent tissue, not the actively dividing one.

questions.prompt: Which simple permanent tissue has thick lignified walls and is usually made of dead cells?
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma has thick lignified walls and gives rigid support; its cells are usually dead at maturity.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing collenchyma — its walls are unevenly thickened but it is a living tissue.

questions.prompt: Which tissue covers body surfaces and lines body cavities?
questions.explanation: Epithelial tissue covers surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands, and rests on connective tissue.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing connective tissue — that supports and binds, but does not primarily cover surfaces.

questions.prompt: Which connective tissue is fluid and transports materials around the body?
questions.explanation: Blood is a fluid connective tissue whose cells are suspended in plasma and which transports materials.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing bone or cartilage — those are solid or firm connective tissues, not fluid ones.

questions.prompt: Which tissue is responsible for movement by contraction?
questions.explanation: Muscular tissue is specialised for contraction and brings about movement in animals.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing nervous tissue — that transmits impulses and coordinates movement rather than producing it directly.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the tissue made of actively dividing cells in plants is called ________ tissue.
questions.explanation: Meristematic tissue is the dividing tissue of plants, found at growing points.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'permanent' — permanent tissue has lost the power of division.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blanks: epithelial tissue always rests on ________ tissue and is separated from it by the ________.
questions.explanation: Epithelium is supported by connective tissue and is anchored to it by the basement membrane.
questions.commonMistake: Answering just 'connective' without naming the basement membrane where both parts are required.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between parenchyma and sclerenchyma on the basis of cell wall and living or dead cells.
questions.answer: Parenchyma has thin cell walls and is made of living cells; it is a simple permanent tissue with thin walls. Sclerenchyma has thick lignified cell walls and its cells are usually dead at maturity; it provides rigid support. So parenchyma is thin-walled and living, while sclerenchyma is thick-walled and usually dead.
questions.explanation: Both the cell wall comparison and the living-or-dead comparison should be given for full marks.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one difference or forgetting to mention lignification in sclerenchyma.

questions.prompt: State the functions of the four main types of animal tissue.
questions.answer: Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands, providing protection and secretion. Connective tissue connects, supports, binds and protects other tissues and organs; examples are bone, cartilage, blood and adipose tissue. Muscular tissue brings about movement by contraction. Nervous tissue transmits impulses and coordinates body activities.
questions.explanation: Each tissue type should be named with its main function; a location can be included for clarity.
questions.commonMistake: Omitting one of the four tissue types or giving only a location without the function.

questions.prompt: Describe meristematic tissue and explain how it differs from permanent tissue.
questions.answer: Meristematic tissue is made of cells that are actively dividing. Its cells are generally small, have dense cytoplasm, a large prominent nucleus and thin cell walls, and they are found in special growing regions of the plant such as the apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots and the lateral meristems such as the cambium. By repeated division, meristematic tissue produces new cells that later form permanent tissues. Permanent tissue differs in that its cells have lost the power to divide and have acquired a definite shape, size and function. Permanent tissues may be simple, like parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma, or complex, like xylem and phloem. Thus the main differences are that meristematic tissue divides actively and has the typical features of young, undifferentiated cells, while permanent tissue is non-dividing and specialised for a particular role.
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes meristematic structure and location, then contrasts division, shape and specialisation with permanent tissue.
questions.commonMistake: Listing only one difference or forgetting to mention that permanent tissues come from meristematic cells.

questions.prompt: A student says that bone is not a tissue because it is hard. Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.answer: I do not agree. Bone is a tissue — specifically a connective tissue — because it is made of cells embedded in a solid, hard matrix of calcium salts and collagen fibres, and it performs the connective-tissue functions of support, protection and binding. Hardness does not disqualify it from being a tissue; hardness is one of the properties of this particular connective tissue. Cartilage is also a connective tissue but is flexible, and blood is a connective tissue even though it is fluid, which shows that connective tissues can have very different consistencies.
questions.explanation: The answer must defend bone as a connective tissue by structure and function, and use the variety of connective tissues to show that hardness alone does not decide the question.
questions.commonMistake: Saying bone is an organ but not explaining why it is also made of connective tissue; the tissue-level classification is what the question tests.
